name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q01 - Linkage between nucleotides in a DNA strand

questiontext.text: In a DNA strand the nucleotides are linked together by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a polynucleotide chain formed by the polymerisation of deoxyribonucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a deoxyribose pentose sugar, and a phosphate group.

Step 2: Evaluation
During DNA strand formation, the \(3'\)-hydroxyl (\(-OH\)) group of the deoxyribose sugar of one nucleotide reacts with the \(5'\)-phosphate group of the adjacent nucleotide. This condensation reaction forms a \(3'\text{--}5'\) phosphodiester bond that creates the sugar-phosphate backbone of the DNA strand. By contrast, glycosidic bonds link the nitrogenous base to the \(1'\) carbon of the sugar, peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins, and hydrogen bonds hold the two complementary strands together across nitrogenous bases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nucleotides in a DNA strand are linked together by phosphodiester bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q02 - Structural difference between nucleoside and nucleotide

questiontext.text: A nucleoside differs from a nucleotide. It lacks the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acids are built from monomeric units called nucleotides, which are phosphorylated nucleosides.

Step 2: Evaluation
A nucleoside is composed of a nitrogenous base linked to a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) via an N-glycosidic linkage. When a phosphate group is attached to the \(5'\)-OH of a nucleoside through a phosphoester linkage, a corresponding nucleotide is formed. Therefore, a nucleoside contains both a base and a sugar (with hydroxyl groups), and lacks the phosphate group.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A nucleoside differs from a nucleotide because it lacks the phosphate group.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q03 - Classification of deoxyribose and ribose sugars

questiontext.text: Both deoxyribose and ribose belong to a class of sugars called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Monosaccharides are classified according to the number of carbon atoms in their backbone: trioses (3 carbons), tetroses (4 carbons), pentoses (5 carbons), and hexoses (6 carbons).

Step 2: Evaluation
Ribose (\(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_5\)) and deoxyribose (\(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_4\)) each contain five carbon atoms arranged in a furanose ring structure in nucleic acids. They are simple monosaccharides rather than polysaccharides.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both deoxyribose and ribose belong to the class of sugars called pentoses.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q04 - Effect of purine pyrimidine base pairing

questiontext.text: The fact that a purine base always pairs through hydrogen bonds with a pyrimidine base in the DNA double helix leads to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Watson-Crick double helix model of DNA, purines (adenine and guanine) are double-ringed nitrogenous bases, whereas pyrimidines (cytosine and thymine) are single-ringed nitrogenous bases.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because a double-ringed purine always pairs with a single-ringed pyrimidine (\(\text{A}=\text{T}\) and \(\text{G}\equiv\text{C}\)), every base pair spans a total of three rings. This generates an approximately uniform distance between the two sugar-phosphate backbones, maintaining a constant diameter of about \(2.0\text{ nm}\) (\(20\text{ \AA}\)) along the entire DNA double helix. Antiparallel polarity arises from opposite \(5'\to 3'\) and \(3'\to 5'\) strand orientations, and semiconservative replication arises from complementary template-directed synthesis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Purine-pyrimidine base pairing leads to a uniform width throughout DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q05 - Net electric charge on DNA and histones

questiontext.text: The net electric charge on DNA and histones is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In eukaryotic cells, DNA is packaged into nucleosomes by wrapping around an octamer of histone proteins through electrostatic attraction.

Step 2: Evaluation
DNA carries a net negative charge due to the ionised phosphate groups (\(\text{PO}_4^{3-}\)) present along its sugar-phosphate backbone. Histones are basic proteins rich in the positively charged amino acid residues lysine and arginine, which give histones a net positive charge at physiological pH. This opposite charge allows DNA to wrap tightly around the positively charged histone octamer.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The net electric charge on DNA and histones is negative and positive, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q06 - Location of promoter and terminator in transcription unit

questiontext.text: The promoter site and the terminator site for transcription are located at:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A transcription unit in DNA consists of three regions: a promoter, the structural gene, and a terminator. By convention, positions along a transcription unit are defined with reference to the polarity of the coding strand (\(5'\to 3'\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
With respect to the coding strand, the promoter is located towards the \(5'\)-end (upstream) of the structural gene, where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. The terminator is located towards the \(3'\)-end (downstream) of the coding strand and defines the end of transcription.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The promoter site and terminator site are located at the \(5'\) (upstream) end and \(3'\) (downstream) end, respectively, of the transcription unit.

answer.text: 3' (downstream) end and 5' (upstream) end, respectively of the transcription unit
5' (upstream) end and 3' (downstream) end, respectively of the transcription unit

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q07 - Characteristics of sickle cell anaemia

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is the most appropriate for sickle cell anaemia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sickle cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a single-base point mutation in the \(\beta\)-globin gene of haemoglobin, substituting glutamic acid with valine at the sixth position of the \(\beta\)-globin chain.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because it results from an inherited structural defect in the haemoglobin molecule rather than an iron deficiency, it is classified as a molecular disease and cannot be cured or treated with iron supplements. Furthermore, individuals who are heterozygous carriers of the sickle cell allele (\(\text{Hb}^A\text{Hb}^S\)) exhibit a selective advantage by having increased resistance against severe malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All of the stated characteristics apply to sickle cell anaemia.

answer.text: It cannot be treated with iron supplements

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q08 - Properties of the AUG codon

questiontext.text: Which of the following is true with respect to AUG?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The genetic code is nearly universal and unambiguous, with specific codons serving dual roles in translation initiation and amino acid specification.

Step 2: Evaluation
The codon AUG has dual functions: it acts as the initiator codon for translation and it codes exclusively for the amino acid methionine (Met). Because the genetic code is nearly universal across organisms, AUG codes for methionine in both prokaryotes (formyl-methionine at initiation, methionine internally) and eukaryotes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All of the stated properties are true with respect to AUG.

answer.text: It codes for methionine in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q09 - Identity of the first genetic material

questiontext.text: The first genetic material could be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the RNA world hypothesis, the earliest self-replicating life forms required a molecule capable of both storing genetic information and catalysing biochemical reactions.

Step 2: Evaluation
RNA is considered the first genetic material because it can store genetic information and also act as a biological catalyst (ribozyme) for essential life processes such as metabolism, translation, and splicing. DNA later evolved from RNA with chemical modifications (deoxyribose sugar and thymine) that made it more stable for long-term information storage. Proteins and carbohydrates do not serve as primary self-replicating genetic material.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first genetic material could be RNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q10 - Exons and introns in mature eukaryotic mRNA

questiontext.text: With regard to mature mRNA in eukaryotes:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In eukaryotes, the primary transcript (hnRNA) contains both coding sequences (exons) and non-coding intervening sequences (introns) and undergoes post-transcriptional processing before becoming mature mRNA.

Step 2: Evaluation
During RNA splicing, the non-coding introns are excised from the hnRNA and the coding exons are joined together in a defined order. Along with \(5'\)-capping and \(3'\)-polyadenylation, this produces the functional mature mRNA that exits the nucleus for translation. Consequently, mature mRNA contains exons but lacks introns.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In mature mRNA in eukaryotes, exons appear but introns do not appear.

answer.text: exons and introns do not appear in the mature RNA
exons appear but introns do not appear in the mature RNA
introns appear but exons do not appear in the mature RNA
both exons and introns appear in the mature RNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q11 - Human chromosomes with highest and least genes

questiontext.text: The human chromosome with the highest and least number of genes in them are respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project mapped and sequenced the 24 different human chromosomes (22 autosomes plus X and Y) and determined the gene distribution across each chromosome.

Step 2: Evaluation
Among all human chromosomes, Chromosome 1 is the largest and contains the highest number of genes (2968 genes), whereas the Y chromosome is much smaller and contains the fewest genes (231 genes).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The human chromosomes with the highest and least number of genes are Chromosome 1 and Y, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q12 - Scientists unrelated to DNA double helix model

questiontext.text: Who amongst the following scientists had no contribution in the development of the double helix model for the structure of DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix model of DNA structure by integrating X-ray diffraction data and base-composition rules established by earlier researchers.

Step 2: Evaluation
Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins produced the X-ray diffraction data (including Photo 51) that revealed the helical geometry and dimensions of DNA. Erwin Chargaff discovered the base-pairing equivalence rules (\(\text{A}=\text{T}\) and \(\text{G}=\text{C}\)). In contrast, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl conducted experiments in 1958 using heavy nitrogen (\({}^{15}\text{N}\)) in E. coli to prove that DNA replicates semiconservatively, which occurred after the double helix model was already established.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Meselson and Stahl had no contribution to the development of the double helix model for the structure of DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q13 - Modification preventing nucleotide polymerisation in DNA

questiontext.text: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides which are linked to each other by 3'-5' phosphodiester bond. To prevent polymerisation of nucleotides, which of the following modifications would you choose?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chain elongation during DNA synthesis proceeds in the \(5'\to 3'\) direction when DNA polymerase catalyses a nucleophilic attack by the free \(3'\text{-OH}\) group of the growing DNA strand on the \(\alpha\)-phosphate of an incoming deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate (dNTP).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because a free \(3'\text{-OH}\) group on the deoxyribose sugar is strictly required to form the next \(3'\text{--}5'\) phosphodiester bond, removing or replacing the \(3'\text{-OH}\) group (as in dideoxynucleotides) terminates chain elongation and prevents further polymerisation. Deoxyribose already lacks a \(2'\text{-OH}\) group (it has a hydrogen atom at the \(2'\) position), and replacing purines with pyrimidines does not block phosphodiester bond formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
To prevent polymerisation of nucleotides, one would remove or replace the \(3'\text{-OH}\) group in deoxyribose.

answer.text: Remove/Replace 2' OH group with some other group in deoxy ribose

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q14 - Cause of discontinuous DNA synthesis

questiontext.text: Discontinuous synthesis of DNA occurs in one strand, because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The two strands of a DNA double helix are antiparallel, and DNA-dependent DNA polymerase can polymerise deoxyribonucleotides in only one direction.

Step 2: Evaluation
DNA-dependent DNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation strictly in the \(5'\to 3'\) direction. At the replication fork, the template strand with \(3'\to 5'\) polarity allows continuous synthesis of the leading strand in the \(5'\to 3'\) direction toward the fork. Conversely, on the template strand with \(5'\to 3'\) polarity, the polymerase must synthesise DNA in the \(5'\to 3'\) direction away from the advancing fork, producing short Okazaki fragments discontinuously that are later joined by DNA ligase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Discontinuous synthesis occurs on one strand because DNA-dependent DNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation only in one direction (\(5'\to 3'\)).

answer.text: DNA molecule being synthesised is very long
DNA dependent DNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation only in one direction (5' → 3')
DNA ligase joins the short stretches of DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q15 - Step in transcription catalysed by RNA polymerase

questiontext.text: Which of the following steps in transcription is catalysed by RNA polymerase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Prokaryotic transcription proceeds through three stages: initiation, elongation, and termination, involving the core RNA polymerase enzyme and accessory protein factors.

Step 2: Evaluation
The core RNA polymerase enzyme is only capable of catalysing the process of elongation (the template-dependent polymerisation of ribonucleoside triphosphates). To initiate transcription at the promoter and to terminate transcription at the terminator, RNA polymerase must associate transiently with the initiation factor sigma (\(\sigma\)) and the termination factor rho (\(\rho\)), respectively.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Elongation is the step in transcription catalysed by RNA polymerase.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q16 - Level of gene expression control in prokaryotes

questiontext.text: Control of gene expression in prokaryotes take place at the level of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In prokaryotes, transcription and translation are coupled in the cytoplasm, and mRNA molecules generally have short lifespans.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, regulating the rate of transcriptional initiation is the predominant and most energetically efficient point for controlling gene expression in prokaryotes (for example, via operon systems such as the lac operon).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Control of gene expression in prokaryotes takes place predominantly at the level of transcription.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q17 - Role of regulatory proteins in prokaryotic transcription

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct about the role of regulatory proteins in transcription in prokaryotes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In prokaryotes, accessibility of the promoter region of DNA to RNA polymerase is modulated by the interaction of accessory regulatory proteins with specific DNA sequences (such as operators).

Step 2: Evaluation
Regulatory proteins can exert either positive or negative control over transcription. When a regulatory protein enhances RNA polymerase binding and increases transcription, it acts as an activator (positive regulation). When it binds to the operator to block RNA polymerase progression and decrease transcription, it acts as a repressor (negative regulation).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Regulatory proteins in prokaryotic transcription can act both as activators and as repressors.

answer.text: They interact with RNA polymerase but do not affect the expression
They can act both as activators and as repressors

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q18 - Last human chromosome to be completely sequenced

questiontext.text: Which was the last human chromosome to be completely sequenced:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project aimed to determine the complete nucleotide sequence of all human chromosomes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Although the draft human genome was published earlier, the finishing of individual chromosomes continued until Chromosome 1—the largest human chromosome—was completely sequenced in May 2006, making it the last of the 24 human chromosomes to be completed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chromosome 1 was the last human chromosome to be completely sequenced.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q19 - Functions of different types of RNA

questiontext.text: Which of the following are the functions of RNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cells contain three major functional classes of RNA involved in protein synthesis: messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

Step 2: Evaluation
Messenger RNA (mRNA) acts as the template that carries genetic information from DNA to the ribosomes for polypeptide synthesis. Transfer RNA (tRNA) acts as an adapter molecule that reads the genetic code and brings specific amino acids to the ribosome. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) serves structural and catalytic roles as a constituent component of ribosomes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All of the listed functions are performed by RNA.

answer.text: It is a carrier of genetic information from DNA to ribosomes synthesising polypeptides.
It is a constituent component of ribosomes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q20 - Applying Chargaff rule to DNA base proportions

questiontext.text: While analysing the DNA of an organism a total number of 5386 nucleotides were found out of which the proportion of different bases were: Adenine = 29%, Guanine = 17%, Cytosine = 32%, Thymine = 17%. Considering the Chargaff's rule it can be concluded that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total nucleotides \(= 5386\). Base proportions: Adenine (\(\text{A}\)) \(= 29\%\), Guanine (\(\text{G}\)) \(= 17\%\), Cytosine (\(\text{C}\)) \(= 32\%\), and Thymine (\(\text{T}\)) \(= 17\%\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume the nucleic acid is DNA (since thymine is present) and evaluate whether it conforms to Watson-Crick double-stranded base pairing.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA, the molar percentage of adenine equals that of thymine (\(\%\text{A} = \%\text{T}\)), and the molar percentage of guanine equals that of cytosine (\(\%\text{G} = \%\text{C}\)), giving \(\frac{\text{A}+\text{G}}{\text{T}+\text{C}} = 1\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the complementary base percentages:
\(\%\text{A} = 29\%\) whereas \(\%\text{T} = 17\%\), so \(\%\text{A} \neq \%\text{T}\).
\(\%\text{G} = 17\%\) whereas \(\%\text{C} = 32\%\), so \(\%\text{G} \neq \%\text{C}\).
Furthermore, \(\text{A} + \text{G} = 29\% + 17\% = 46\%\), while \(\text{T} + \text{C} = 17\% + 32\% = 49\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since the base composition violates Chargaff's equivalence rule (\(\text{A}=\text{T}\) and \(\text{G}=\text{C}\)) required for double-stranded DNA, the DNA molecule cannot be double-stranded (either linear or circular). Therefore, it is single-stranded DNA.

answer.text: it is a double stranded circular DNA
It is a double stranded linear DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q21 - DNA synthesised from an RNA template in viruses

questiontext.text: In some viruses, DNA is synthesised by using RNA as template. Such a DNA is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain viruses, known as retroviruses, carry RNA as their genetic material and use the enzyme reverse transcriptase to synthesise DNA from an RNA template (reverse transcription).

Step 2: Evaluation
The DNA molecule synthesised by reverse transcription using an RNA template is complementary to the RNA sequence and is therefore termed complementary DNA (cDNA). By contrast, A-DNA and B-DNA are structural conformations of double-stranded DNA, and rDNA refers to recombinant DNA (or ribosomal DNA).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
DNA synthesised using RNA as a template is called cDNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q22 - Ratio of DNA types after four generations in Meselson Stahl

questiontext.text: If Meselson and Stahl's experiment is continued for four generations in bacteria, the ratio of \(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{15}\): \(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{14}\): \(\text{N}^{14}/\text{N}^{14}\) containing DNA in the fourth generation would be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Parent bacteria contain heavy DNA (\(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{15}\)) and are allowed to replicate in a light nitrogen (\(\text{N}^{14}\)) medium for \(n = 4\) generations.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
DNA replication is semiconservative: each DNA duplex separates into two parental strands, and each strand acts as a template for synthesising a new \(\text{N}^{14}\) strand.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Starting from 1 heavy DNA molecule (\(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{15}\)), after \(n\) generations the total number of DNA molecules is \(2^n\). The two original \(\text{N}^{15}\) strands remain conserved in 2 hybrid molecules (\(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{14}\)), while all remaining molecules are light (\(\text{N}^{14}/\text{N}^{14}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(n = 4\) generations:
Total DNA molecules \(= 2^4 = 16\).
Number of \(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{15}\) molecules \(= 0\).
Number of \(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{14}\) (hybrid) molecules \(= 2\).
Number of \(\text{N}^{14}/\text{N}^{14}\) (light) molecules \(= 16 - 2 = 14\).
The ratio is \(0 : 2 : 14\), which simplifies by dividing by 2 to \(0 : 1 : 7\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Summing the parts: \(0 + 1 + 7 = 8\) (representing \(0\%\) heavy, \(12.5\%\) hybrid, and \(87.5\%\) light DNA). The ratio of \(\text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{15} : \text{N}^{15}/\text{N}^{14} : \text{N}^{14}/\text{N}^{14}\) in the fourth generation is \(0:1:7\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q23 - RNA transcript sequence from DNA coding strand

questiontext.text:
If the sequence of nitrogen bases of the coding strand of DNA in a transcription unit is:
5' - A T G A A T G - 3',
the sequence of bases in its RNA transcript would be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The given DNA coding strand sequence is \(5'\text{ - A T G A A T G - }3'\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Transcription produces a single-stranded RNA molecule in the \(5'\to 3'\) direction using the complementary template strand (\(3'\to 5'\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Because the coding strand and the RNA transcript are both complementary to the same template strand and share the same \(5'\to 3'\) polarity, the RNA transcript has the exact same base sequence as the DNA coding strand, except that thymine (\(\text{T}\)) is replaced by uracil (\(\text{U}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Determine the template strand complementary to the coding strand:
Coding strand: \(5'\text{ - A T G A A T G - }3'\)
Template strand: \(3'\text{ - T A C T T A C - }5'\)
2. Transcribe the template strand into RNA using base-pairing rules (\(\text{A}\to\text{U}\), \(\text{T}\to\text{A}\), \(\text{G}\to\text{C}\), \(\text{C}\to\text{G}\)):
RNA transcript: \(5'\text{ - A U G A A U G - }3'\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Comparing directly with the coding strand \(5'\text{ - A T G A A T G - }3'\), replacing \(\text{T}\) with \(\text{U}\) gives \(5'\text{ - A U G A A U G - }3'\).

answer.text: 5' - A U G A A U G - 3'
5' - U A C U U A C - 3'
5' - C A U U C A U - 3'
5' - G U A A G U A - 3'

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q24 - Regions transcribed by RNA polymerase holoenzyme

questiontext.text: The RNA polymerase holoenzyme transcribes:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A prokaryotic transcription unit contains a promoter, a structural gene, and a terminator.

Step 2: Evaluation
The RNA polymerase holoenzyme (core enzyme + \(\sigma\) factor) recognises and binds to the promoter region to initiate transcription, but the promoter itself serves only as a binding site and is not transcribed. Transcription begins at the transcription start site and proceeds through the structural gene, continuing until the polymerase reaches and transcribes through the terminator region, where the termination factor (\(\rho\)) or terminator structure causes release of the nascent RNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The RNA polymerase holoenzyme transcribes the structural gene and the terminator region.

answer.text: the promoter, structural gene and the terminator region
the structural gene and the terminator region

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q25 - Sequence of tRNA anticodon pairing with mRNA codon

questiontext.text: If the base sequence of a codon in mRNA is 5'-AUG-3', the sequence of tRNA pairing with it must be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The mRNA codon sequence is \(5'\text{-AUG-}3'\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Codon-anticodon pairing between mRNA and tRNA follows Watson-Crick complementary base pairing in an antiparallel orientation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In RNA-RNA pairing, \(\text{A}\) pairs with \(\text{U}\), and \(\text{G}\) pairs with \(\text{C}\). If the mRNA codon is read \(5'\to 3'\), the complementary tRNA anticodon runs \(3'\to 5'\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
mRNA codon: \(5'\text{ - A U G - }3'\)
Antiparallel tRNA anticodon: \(3'\text{ - U A C - }5'\)
Reversing the \(3'\text{ - U A C - }5'\) sequence to write it in the standard \(5'\to 3'\) convention gives \(5'\text{ - CAU - }3'\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Reading \(5'\text{ - CAU - }3'\) in reverse (\(3'\to 5'\)) yields \(3'\text{ - UAC - }5'\), which is complementary and antiparallel to \(5'\text{ - AUG - }3'\). Thus, the tRNA sequence is \(5'\text{ - CAU - }3'\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q26 - Site of amino acid attachment on tRNA

questiontext.text: The amino acid attaches to the tRNA at its:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transfer RNA (tRNA) is an adapter molecule with a cloverleaf secondary structure and an L-shaped tertiary structure, possessing distinct functional regions for codon recognition and amino acid binding.

Step 2: Evaluation
Every tRNA has an anticodon loop that base-pairs with the mRNA codon, and an amino acid acceptor end located at the \(3'\)-end (terminating in the conserved \(5'\text{-CCA-}3'\) sequence). During aminoacylation (charging of tRNA), the specific amino acid is covalently linked to the \(3'\)-end of the tRNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The amino acid attaches to the tRNA at its \(3'\)-end.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q27 - Ribosomal subunit binding to mRNA during initiation

questiontext.text: To initiate translation, the mRNA first binds to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Translation is the process of polymerising amino acids to form a polypeptide on ribosomes, beginning with an ordered assembly of the initiation complex.

Step 2: Evaluation
When the smaller ribosomal subunit encounters the mRNA (along with the initiator tRNA carrying methionine), translation of the mRNA to protein begins. Only after the smaller ribosomal subunit binds to the mRNA and aligns with the start codon does the larger ribosomal subunit join to form the complete, functional ribosome.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
To initiate translation, the mRNA first binds to the smaller ribosomal sub-unit.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULARBASISOFINHERITANCE_MCQ_Q28 - Mechanism of switching on the lac operon

questiontext.text: In E.coli, the lac operon gets switched on when:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The lac operon in E. coli is an inducible operon regulated negatively by a repressor protein encoded by the \(i\) gene.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the absence of an inducer, the repressor protein binds to the operator region and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes (\(z\), \(y\), and \(a\)). When lactose (specifically its isomer allolactose) is present, it acts as an inducer and binds to the repressor protein, causing a conformational change that inactivates the repressor. The inactivated repressor can no longer bind to the operator, allowing RNA polymerase access to the promoter so that transcription of the lac operon proceeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In E. coli, the lac operon gets switched on when lactose is present and it binds to the repressor.

answer.text: lactose is present and it binds to the repressor
lactose is present and it binds to RNA polymerase
